title: Foldsmith+
summary: A papercraft design tool with 3D previews, folding instructions, and printable cutting sheets.
contribution: Studio direction and review; implementation and technical cross-review by Codex and Claude Code.

sections.title: The idea
paragraphs: A design tool has to carry an idea all the way to a usable artifact. Foldsmith turns a collection of 61 papercraft designs into adjustable projects: change dimensions and colors, examine the assembly in 3D, then export a coordinated kit of instructions and full-size cutting sheets.

sections.title: One model, several representations
paragraphs: The preview, attachment labels and exported sheets come from the same built kit. Global print scale is explicit, a calibration square travels with the sheets, and dimensions that cannot produce a valid net become a diagnostic instead of a silently distorted template. Portable project files and undo/redo make experimentation recoverable.

Design mode accepts constrained proposals through the same geometry and print checks. The optional private AI helper drafts within that vocabulary; the regular collection and manual editor work without model access.

sections.title: How it was built
paragraphs: Codex and Claude Code collaborated on geometry, the workshop, catalog, exports and integration review. My review included pushing beyond decorative approximations toward actual shaped solids. The interesting boundary is between a convincing rendering and a printable construction: both need to describe the same object.

limitations: Digital geometry checks do not establish physical craftability, material strength or wearer comfort.
The optional AI helper uses private access; the public collection is independently usable.
imageAlt: Foldsmith workshop with an editable papercraft model, assembly preview and export controls.

title: Lanternfish LF-16
eyebrow: A computer small enough to inspect
summary: A 16-bit fantasy computer with its own language, compiler, emulator, IDE, and debugger.
contribution: Studio direction and review; implementation and technical cross-review by Codex and Claude Code.

sections.title: The idea
paragraphs: Build a complete computer whose layers remain small enough to follow. The LF-16 starts with an original instruction set and memory-mapped devices, then adds an assembler, the C-like Glint language, a monitor ROM and a browser IDE. Its games and music tools run on the machine it defines.

sections.title: From source to behavior
paragraphs: The IDE connects source code to live machine state. Breakpoints, stepping, disassembly, registers, memory and serial output provide different views of the same execution. Glint source maps make the compiler output inspectable; assembly cartridges expose individual instructions.

The deliberately bounded machine has 64 KiB of memory, a 160 × 120 display, a 16-color palette and four audio voices. Original cartridges include Lumen Drift, Tidepool, Prism Courier and Abyss Tracker. Source and cartridge import/export let the environment serve as a workshop as well as a demo.

sections.title: The collaboration
paragraphs: Claude Code led the ISA, emulator, assembler, IDE and assembly programs. Codex built the Glint compiler, monitor ROM, puzzle game and tracker. Each reviewed the other’s components. The integration question was concrete: could independently built toolchain layers agree well enough to execute and debug real programs?

limitations: Glint intentionally omits features such as floating point and structs; there is no separate linker.
Audio is a software approximation, and the editing experience is best on desktop.
imageAlt: Lanternfish IDE showing source code, a running cartridge, registers and machine state.

title: Signal Garden
eyebrow: Music you can read as a landscape
summary: A visual music composition tool where an editable landscape controls the score.
contribution: Studio direction and review; implementation and technical cross-review by Codex and Claude Code.

sections.title: The idea
paragraphs: Make a musical arrangement visible without replacing composition with a decorative visualizer. Four instrument beds become layers of a living garden. Horizontal position follows time, height follows pitch, and phrasing and level affect the shapes. The score remains readable while playback is paused.

sections.title: An instrument with memory
paragraphs: The editor supports sections, repeated bars, chords, velocity, note length, meter and instrument choices. A seeded composer develops motifs into complete arrangements. Separate visual controls change the scenery while preserving the music.

Live playback and offline WAV export share synthesis and event rules. Portable JSON, independent working drafts, migration, undo/redo and explicit storage warnings treat a composition as work worth keeping. The responsive layout preserves the garden while tools move into a dock or drawer on smaller screens.

sections.title: The collaboration
paragraphs: Codex led the sequencer, synthesis and export; Claude Code built the visual world, interface and authored pieces. Their shared boundary was the score: one representation had to drive sound, editing, animation and saved files consistently. Automated audio and interaction checks support that contract, while musical taste still requires listening.

limitations: No MIDI, microphone recording, plugin hosting or cloud synchronization.
Background playback depends on browser behavior; automated checks cannot establish musical quality.
imageAlt: Signal Garden showing a luminous musical landscape alongside note beds and composition controls.

title: Parlour
summary: A multiplayer party-game platform with shared-scene memory and collaborative invention games.
contribution: Studio direction and review; implementation and technical cross-review by Codex and Claude Code.

sections.title: Two games, one session system
paragraphs: False Witness asks players to remember a shared scene while navigating misleading witness reports. Patent Pending turns private constraints into a collective invention and drawing game. Both use one host screen and separate player screens, so information boundaries are part of the rules.

sections.title: The infrastructure behind the room
paragraphs: The server projects a different view for the host and each player. Private credentials, reconnectable event streams, bounded requests, explicit deadlines and durable checkpoints support sessions that outlive a dropped connection. A client recovery ledger distinguishes a confirmed submission from an attempt whose outcome is still unknown.

That distinction matters during play: reconnecting should recover the same player and submitted action rather than invent a second move or expose someone else’s card. Host pacing and expiry rules also keep abandoned sessions from remaining active indefinitely.

sections.title: The collaboration
paragraphs: Codex and Claude Code developed the session foundation, game logic and host/player interfaces as a coordinated Studio project. The implementation separates transport, private views and the game’s own transitions, making it possible to inspect a rule independently of a network interruption.

limitations: The free hosted service can need a cold start.
Current portfolio checks cover the public landing page; group enjoyment and physical-phone play are not established by these checks.
The hosted demo can take a moment to wake up after inactivity.
imageAlt: Parlour’s hosted landing page introducing its host-screen and private-player party games.

title: Tidal Archive
summary: A narrative game about saving a flooded city’s history when the archive has room for only twelve pages.
contribution: Studio direction and review; implementation and technical cross-review by Codex and Claude Code.

sections.title: The idea
paragraphs: Halloway is drowning, and the relief boat leaves in three days. As its last archivist, you explore by tide, recover records, talk to the people who remain and decide what deserves a place in a twelve-page Tidebook. Routes, diving and mechanisms connect the passage of time to the story.

sections.title: A world with explicit rules
paragraphs: A deterministic engine receives commands and produces the current view. The interface does not directly rewrite the world: travel, inventory, puzzle actions and ending conditions share the same state model. The map’s flooding is checked against the engine’s tide rules.

The authored world contains 18 places, 30 documents, five characters, six puzzles and seven endings. Scripted walkthroughs provide witnesses for reaching the endings; versioned saves and portable journey files let a player stop and return. The procedural scene art and synthesized atmosphere respond to location and water level.

sections.title: The collaboration
paragraphs: Claude Code led the city, prose, interface, art and audio. Codex implemented the engine, validation, save semantics and bounded reachability analysis. Their contract joined a narrative author’s intentions to transitions the program could actually execute.

limitations: The general reachability search is bounded; walkthrough witnesses are not an exhaustive proof of every possible playthrough.
Estimated play length and enjoyment have not been established through a human-player study.
imageAlt: Tidal Archive’s flooded city map, current scene, tide clock and narrative choices.

title: Event Horizon
eyebrow: A different clock. A different homecoming.
summary: An orbital flight simulation with black holes, time dilation, and delayed signals.
contribution: Studio direction and review; implementation and technical cross-review by Codex and Claude Code.

sections.title: The idea
paragraphs: Flying close to a black hole changes more than an orbit. Across seven missions, a pilot compares ship, probe and home clocks, plans burns and sends messages to people whose lives continue at a different rate. The homecoming depends on elapsed time and the correspondence that actually arrives.

sections.title: Prediction is not arrival
paragraphs: The flight planner previews maneuvers using the simulation’s own equations. A signal ledger records transmission and reception events; missions with communication consequences resolve from actual arrivals, not from a forecast painted on the interface. Pending signals remain pending.

The presentation exposes the tension through orbit maps, clocks, an optical view and a burn plan. Progressive controls teach a path from manual correction to circularization and finer planning. In one mission, a deeper orbit trades image resolution against getting a photograph home in time.

sections.title: The collaboration
paragraphs: Codex owned physics, predictions, signals and optics; Claude Code built the expedition, interface and narrative. My playtest feedback on the first four missions prompted clearer controls, a visible burn plan and a more gradual introduction to the flight computer.

limitations: This is an authored simulation with declared instrument rules, not an astrophysical research package.
Bounded event searches can remain unresolved; the interface must preserve that uncertainty.
imageAlt: Event Horizon with an orbital map, black-hole optical view, mission brief, burn planner and clocks.

title: Impossible Rooms
summary: A first-person exploration game with folded corridors, nested rooms, and impossible geometry.
contribution: Studio direction and review; implementation and technical cross-review by Codex and Claude Code.

sections.title: The idea
paragraphs: A closet opens into a cathedral. A corridor brings you home after three turns. A miniature house contains another miniature of itself. Impossible Rooms turns transformations into an exploration game: find lanterns, mark the moments that seem wrong and compare your observations when the house ends.

sections.title: Geometry with an intentional contradiction
paragraphs: Each room is ordinary Euclidean geometry in its own frame. Doorways join those frames through rigid transforms and, for nested rooms, uniform scale. A seeded generator composes several architectural wings from nine kinds of spatial impossibility.

A recursive portal renderer maintains the view across doorways, while the world model checks reachability and records contradictions in the map. Ariadne’s thread follows the player through the rooms, so it can reappear somewhere it seems unable to belong. Architect mode lets visitors choose the ingredients of a house.

sections.title: The collaboration
paragraphs: Claude Code led the experience, renderer and world presentation; Codex contributed topology and validity checking. The shared problem was to make the space impossible in the intended way while keeping traversal, goals and rendering coherent enough to explore.

limitations: Recursive rendering is bounded by depth and frame-time budgets.
Performance and motion comfort vary by device; browser load checks do not replace extended playtesting.
imageAlt: A first-person view inside Impossible Rooms, with richly lit architecture and connected doorways.

title: Worldseed
eyebrow: Change one assumption. Follow the difference.
summary: A procedural ecosystem simulation for comparing how different choices change a world.
contribution: Studio direction and review; implementation and technical cross-review by Codex and Claude Code.

sections.title: The idea
paragraphs: Watch a small world develop across 120 epochs, then fork its history: remove an ice age, change a land bridge or prevent a predator’s arrival. Compare descendant species, follow trait differences and enter the same region under two histories.

sections.title: A comparison that means something
paragraphs: Worldseed uses explicit, bounded ecology and trait rules. Randomness is keyed by seed, epoch, lineage, region and purpose rather than consumed from one shared stream. A fork therefore avoids shifting unrelated random draws merely because another event occurred.

Branch storage, deterministic replay and causal traces support the comparison. The atlas exposes species ranges and event history; the cousins view connects related lineages across branches. Published rules explain what the toy world actually computes. This framing makes its limitations part of understanding the system.

sections.title: The collaboration
paragraphs: Claude Code built geography, climate, evolution, creatures and the interface. Codex implemented branching, replay, lineage matching, trace queries and invariants. Together they treated an attractive world and a trustworthy comparison as separate requirements that had to meet.

limitations: The ecology is a deliberately simplified toy, not a validated biological model.
Recorded cold replay performance misses the project’s original target; some extinction behavior remains narrower than intended.
The atlas is best explored on desktop; the current mobile layout can clip dense controls.
imageAlt: Worldseed’s hexagonal atlas, species cards and timeline after advancing the simulation.

title: Afterimage
summary: Explore a courtyard across four eras, change its history, and collect evidence of what happened.
contribution: Studio direction and review; implementation and technical cross-review by Codex and Claude Code.

sections.title: The idea
paragraphs: Chandler’s Court can be visited in 1926, 1958, 1991 and 2026. Small choices change what survives: buildings, objects and the people who remember them. The player’s notebook separates direct observations, testimony and personal theories rather than presenting every interpretation as a fact.

sections.title: History and evidence are separate systems
paragraphs: Six authored choices produce a bounded set of possible histories. A deterministic engine replays prerequisites and records their values; content checks catch dependency cycles, incompatible types and competing writers. A counterfactual comparison holds other selections fixed when examining a single choice.

The player does not receive the developer’s complete causal trace. Notebook comparisons show collected observations, preserve earlier wording and leave an uninspected history blank. Accounts told to Maya require evidence available in the current history, while older accounts remain labeled as such. Portable exports carry that distinction into a readable notebook.

sections.title: The collaboration
paragraphs: Codex and Claude Code jointly developed the causal engine, evidence semantics, authored place and story. Their integration reviews focused on whether the experience could support interpretation without silently turning testimony or hindsight into ground truth.

limitations: The history is authored fiction, not a reconstruction of a real place.
An independent agent probe covered one ending and recovery paths, not every possible narrative route.
imageAlt: Afterimage’s brick courtyard in 2026, rendered as a first-person historical exploration scene.

title: Glyphcraft / Kettle Pass
eyebrow: Read a language. Make it your own.
summary: An invented-script game and authoring tool with grammar rules and font export.
contribution: Studio direction and review; implementation and technical cross-review by Codex and Claude Code.

sections.title: The idea
paragraphs: In a mountain keeper’s hut, a trail stone, tally stick and unfinished note offer clues to an unfamiliar script. Read the signs, compose a reply and reshape the letters. The companion workshop extends the premise into a tool for making a small writing system of your own.

sections.title: Changes have consequences
paragraphs: Letter geometry, word mappings and declared sentence patterns remain distinct. Before a word or rule changes, the workshop lists affected lines. A line that no longer fits becomes unresolved until the author repairs it, rather than retaining an old translation that the new rules cannot justify.

The ledger separates drafts from accepted versions. Exports use an accepted project; quoted writing preserves its author’s words even when the current script changes. The project can produce a real TrueType font and a portable script bundle, while a standalone writing page carries accepted forms into the browser or printer.

sections.title: The collaboration
paragraphs: Codex developed language, workspace, geometry and export foundations. Claude Code built the Kettle Pass story, hut interaction and authoring workshop. Their common boundary was meaning: editing the visual system should not quietly rewrite another author’s words.

limitations: The grammar is a declared toy language, not a general-purpose translator.
Exported fonts use Private Use Area mappings and do not supply a universal keyboard or shaping system.
imageAlt: Glyphcraft’s Kettle Pass hut with a primer, handwritten script, a note and a tally stick.

title: Surveyor / Windbreak Ridge
eyebrow: A map someone else must trust
summary: A terrain surveying and mapmaking game where a courier navigates using your field sheet.
contribution: Studio direction and review; implementation and technical cross-review by Codex and Claude Code.

sections.title: The idea
paragraphs: Oriel has a delivery to make and your map is all they have. Take bearings from survey pins, decide what you saw, mark the destination and draw a route. The return report becomes evidence for revising the sheet, rather than an automatic correction to the world’s true coordinates.

sections.title: An information boundary you can play
paragraphs: The traveler receives the player’s map and short-range movement feedback. Hidden terrain stays behind a separate adapter. Reports are composed from what happened locally: a blocked route, a visible carving, a bridge that will not carry a loaded cart.

Three main expeditions change the source of difficulty. Windbreak Ridge introduces geometry; Switchback Pass adds a transport constraint; Twin Orchard makes identity as important as a precise bearing. A well-measured location can still be the wrong destination. Portable saves preserve the sheet and completed trips so the explanation can be revisited.

sections.title: The collaboration
paragraphs: Codex built the geometry and traveler core. Claude Code authored the landscape, diorama, sheet and experience, with joint interface review. The project’s central rule—no hidden route oracle for the courier—connects the player’s mistakes to visible, understandable consequences.

limitations: The simulation uses declared geometry and movement assumptions.
Engineering replays and agent probes do not establish physical-device performance or human enjoyment.
The field-sheet interface is best explored on desktop; the current mobile layout can clip dense controls.
imageAlt: Surveyor’s terrain diorama next to the player’s field sheet, survey pins and courier’s note.

title: Automata
eyebrow: Draw the motion. Discover the machine.
summary: A mechanical sculpture tool for designing motion with cams, linkages, and gears.
contribution: Studio direction and review; implementation and technical cross-review by Codex and Claude Code.

sections.title: The idea
paragraphs: Sketch a rise, a pause and a return, then watch a mechanism perform that motion. Automata connects a motion editor to a bench of kinetic sculptures: a pecking bird, a waving cat, a blacksmith, a clock tower and other small mechanical scenes. Relative timing makes their parts interact.

sections.title: Mechanisms with inspectable limits
paragraphs: The core models four-bars, slider-cranks, gear pairs and cams. It separates prepared part geometry from per-frame rigid poses, and moves expensive scans into a worker. Unreachable poses, excessive cam pressure angles and interference become identifiable diagnostics.

Editable dimensions and phase link the sculpture to its mechanism. Dimensioned SVG exports retain one global scale and a calibration mark. A sampled collision check states what was checked; it does not turn a set of clear frames into a proof of continuous clearance.

sections.title: The collaboration
paragraphs: Codex developed kinematics, inverse cam geometry, interference checks and exports. Claude Code built the editor, guidance and eight-sculpture collection. The published browser exposes these tools, while earlier source documentation still records an in-progress product gate; this case study treats the application as a working workshop with explicit physical limits.

limitations: Ideal rigid bodies omit friction, strength, fit and hardware volumes; physical fabrication has not been validated.
Collision clearance is sampled, and the recorded experience-acceptance status is incomplete.
imageAlt: Automata’s kinetic bird sculpture with visible cams, editable mechanism parts and motion timelines.
